bridges.mechanism: Stronger sanctions increase compliance risk for banks and trading counterparties (fear of secondary sanctions), inducing deleveraging and reduced willingness to provide repo or dealer intermediation and thereby narrowing market liquidity.

Tighter, broader sanctions raise compliance costs and banking/payment frictions for firms operating across the US‑Canada corridor, increasing legal/regulatory uncertainty that leads companies to delay or reduce cross‑border investment commitments.

An intensification of sanctions expands legal authorities and political will to close loopholes and to target dual‑use channels, triggering more frequent and stricter export controls, investigations and interdiction actions against AI‑relevant goods and services.

Greater third‑party compliance with sanctions and interdiction efforts directly blocks or freezes financial channels and cargo routes used for covert Iran→Russia transfers of missile components, drones and propellants, thereby reducing the rate at which Russia replenishes ammunition and critical components.

High compliance by third‑party traders and banks cuts off a subset of smaller or niche exporters from key markets, accelerating exits and consolidation so that AI hardware sourcing becomes concentrated among large suppliers operating within compliant jurisdictions.

A rise in attacks and seizures in the Strait of Hormuz raises insurance premiums and forces merchant shippers and private contractors to reroute or suspend voyages and compels allied navies to reassign escort assets, producing measurable delays and reduced volumes of Western arms and munitions shipments into the Ukraine theater.

Visible and sustained disruptions to commercial shipping in the Gulf raise policymakers' and markets' perception that regional conflict dynamics are widening and that third‑party kinetic involvement or naval confrontations are more likely, increasing the perceived risk of escalation around the Russia–Ukraine war.

A rise in Strait of Hormuz shipping disruptions spikes geopolitical risk and intraday volatility, causing dealers to pull back market‑making and hoard balance‑sheet capacity, which reduces the depth and ease of executing large Treasury transactions.

A rise in attacks/seizures/mining in the Strait of Hormuz forces tankers and bulk carriers to divert, increases voyage times and war‑risk insurance/premiums, and therefore produces measurable delays, rerouting and higher freight/transaction costs for supply chains that move seaborne inputs between the US and Canada.

High‑visibility maritime incidents raise domestic political pressure in both countries to demonstrate security/alignment, fueling calls for tougher economic measures or trade postures between US and Canada when one side is perceived as insufficiently responsive.

Escalating maritime disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz raise logistics risk and insurance premiums, prompting cloud providers, hyperscalers and chip buyers to accelerate and reallocate CAPEX into redundant regional data centers, inventory stockpiles and alternative supply routes.

Frequent shipping incidents disproportionately increase operating costs for smaller, geographically dispersed suppliers, favoring large vertically integrated manufacturers and distributors that can absorb logistics risk and thereby concentrating supply in fewer firms.

A decline in Iranian export volumes (notably crude) tightens global oil supply and pushes prices up, increasing Russian energy revenue and fiscal room to procure/produce munitions and sustain higher tempo of offensive strikes in Ukraine.

Higher export volumes from affected suppliers relieve global energy/supply constraints, lowering inflation expectations and the inflation risk premium embedded in long-term Treasury yields, so an increase in exports pushes yields down.

An increase in export volumes from affected suppliers (e.g., restored seaborne crude from sanctioned producers) substitutes for North American sourcing, causing US buyers to import less from Canada and reducing aggregate US‑Canada goods flows.

Targeted retaliatory measures (e.g., selective export controls, expedited customs inspections) applied as part of the bilateral spat can be used to slow or block specific cargo flows—including military consignments transiting the US–Canada border—reducing delivered volumes to the theater.
A spike in punitive measures raises near‑term economic and policy uncertainty, prompting investors to shift into US Treasuries as a safe haven and thereby pushing long‑term yields down.

Targeted retaliatory measures (tariffs, component bans, blocking cross‑border shipments) interrupt deliveries of critical semiconductor inputs to fabs, lowering utilization and near‑term producible accelerator/chip output.

Cross‑border delays, customs slowdowns and rerouting caused by the US–Canada trade spat interrupt just‑in‑time shipments of ammunition components and propellants that feed North American production lines, directly lowering on‑hand munitions and spare‑parts stocks available for Ukraine support.
Material cross‑border supply shocks amplify price volatility and hedging flows, leading dealers to reduce inventory and widen bid/ask spreads, which directly reduces Treasury market liquidity.

Repeated cross‑border delays and higher transaction costs increase project execution risk and expected returns for AI infrastructure, prompting financiers and corporates to delay or withdraw planned capital allocations into the contested ecosystem.

If firms pull or scale back bilateral investments and joint ventures tied to the US‑Canada market, smaller suppliers and new entrants are crowded out, increasing the share held by a few large incumbents and raising market concentration in AI hardware supply.

Rising domestic political pressure in the US or Canada during a trade spat prompts executives or parliaments to delay or withhold approval/funding for arms transfers or export licences for equipment bound for Ukraine, reducing the rate of allied materiel deliveries.

Rising domestic political pressure to protect affected industries and voters increases the likelihood that fiscal or monetary authorities will step in with direct bond purchases or stabilization facilities, raising the intensity of market interventions.

Escalating domestic political pressure in the US/Canada spat pushes policymakers and enforcement agencies to adopt and more frequently apply export‑controls and compliance actions that are explicitly aimed at limiting tech transfers to China.

A rise in long-term sovereign yields raises the cost of borrowing and refinancing for allied governments and defence contractors, prompting near-term budgetary tightening and delayed or reduced external materiel deliveries.
A rise in long-term sovereign yields attracts capital into the currency and raises the exchange rate, making US exports to Canada more expensive and reducing cross‑border trade flows.

Higher long-term yields increase firms' expected cost of long‑duration financing and hurdle rates, causing corporations to delay or cancel capital projects and cross‑border investment commitments in the bilateral market.

Rising long-term yields increase the cost of capital and raise discount rates, disproportionately hurting smaller entrants and startups while advantaging large incumbents with stronger balance sheets and access to liquidity, thus increasing concentration in AI hardware and supplier markets.

A fall in bond-market liquidity causes banks and dealers to hoard cash and withdraw trade‑finance and repo facilities, constraining defence firms' working capital and transport financing and thereby reducing on‑hand munitions, fuel and spare‑parts stocks at the front.

A deterioration in bond market liquidity raises funding and roll‑over risk for banks and trade financiers, prompting tighter trade credit, reduced use of letters of credit and insurance, and thus causing delays and rerouting in cross‑border supply chains.

A sustained increase in sovereign bond issuance absorbs institutional investor allocations into safe, long-duration paper and shortens available private funding for long-horizon AI and hardware projects, reducing new capital deployment into those builds.

Aggressive central‑bank asset purchases and liquidity operations reduce funding stress and FX volatility for correspondent banks and trade finance providers, making them less likely to cut off or de‑risk business and thereby sustaining third‑party compliance with restrictions.

Active market interventions (swap lines, asset purchases, liquidity facilities) stabilize payment and FX channels and free short‑term cash positions for suppliers and recipient governments, enabling immediate acceleration of payments and military shipments.

Direct market interventions (e.g., large-scale Treasury purchases) inject reserves and compress term premia, lowering corporate financing costs and freeing bank/institutional capacity to fund AI infrastructure and data-center projects.
High-tempo strikes that damage physical infrastructure and raise counterparty/settlement risk cause dealers to pull inventories and widen bid-ask spreads, reducing bond market depth and tradability.

A surge in strikes against ports, rail hubs and shipping in the Black Sea and surrounding regions forces rerouting and longer transit times for container and bulk shipments, cascading into delays and higher transaction costs for North American firms that depend on tightly timed international inputs and thereby increasing US‑Canada cross‑border supply frictions.

Visible increases in allied weapon and system shipments to Ukraine raise concern about arms diversion to Russia and prompt policymakers to expand and tighten sanctions and enforcement against suppliers (including Iranian entities) to block transfers.
Larger allied military aid packages delivered as grants or direct materiel reduce the immediate financing needs of the recipient government, lowering near-term sovereign bond issuance.

Sustained allied weapons and logistics flows create explicit demand for secure, onshore dual‑use supply chains, inducing private and public capital commitments into domestic AI hardware fabs, packaging and related infrastructure.

War-driven disruptions to global energy and commodity supplies produce price spikes and supply gaps that incentivize importers and intermediaries to purchase or smuggle more sanctioned Iranian oil/commodities, increasing Iran's export volumes.
Wider economic disruption forces governments to finance emergency relief, reconstruction and energy subsidies, increasing sovereign bond issuance into the market.

Broad economic disruption from sanctions, commodity shocks and disrupted trade routes depresses demand and raises costs for exporters and importers, reducing the flow of goods and services between the US and Canada as firms cut orders and postpone shipments.
Rising perceptions of imminent escalation prompt central banks and treasuries to deploy preemptive bond purchases, liquidity facilities and swap lines to calm funding strains and tail-risk concerns.

Rising perception that the conflict may broaden increases domestic political pressure in both countries to take hardline economic positions (use trade tools for leverage, restrict sensitive transfers), intensifying confrontational rhetoric and demands for retaliatory trade measures in bilateral disputes.

Rising perceptions that the Russia–Ukraine conflict may broaden prompt US/EU policymakers to expand and more actively enforce export controls and sanctions on advanced computing and semiconductors destined for China to limit dual‑use spillovers.

Depletion of ammunition, fuel and spare parts in the Ukraine theater drives covert procurement from sanctioned sources, creating commercial opportunities that lead intermediaries, shippers and banks to loosen compliance and facilitate sanction‑circumventing transactions.

Persistent depletion of ammunition and logistics stocks forces defense prime contractors and tiered suppliers to retool capacity and prioritize urgent domestic contracts, prompting them to delay or cancel planned cross‑border capital projects and investments in Canada.

A sharp rise in demand for advanced AI compute raises the perceived dual‑use risk of high‑end chips and accelerators, prompting governments to expand the scope and tightness of sanctions/export controls that can be applied to Iran to prevent military/AI applications.

Sustained inflows of capital into non‑Western chip/hardware production and alternative finance in China and allied markets create viable suppliers and payment channels that third parties can use to evade Western restrictions, reducing overall compliance with sanctions on Iran.
A surge of capital into onshoring AI hardware and supply-chain capacity in the US redirects procurement away from Canadian suppliers, directly reducing bilateral goods and component trade flows.

An increase in global AI accelerator and vision-processor manufacturing capacity lowers unit costs and expands availability of components used in loitering munitions, comms/autonomy kits and seekers, enabling faster fielding or replenishment of UAV/precision strike stocks and thus raising the tempo of kinetic strikes.

A fall in producible AI hardware capacity (e.g., curtailed chip output) directly produces component shortages that force rerouting, delays and higher transaction costs across North American supply chains, increasing US–Canada supply disruptions (conversely, capacity growth reduces disruption).

Greater concentration of critical AI/hardware supply in a few firms (especially in jurisdictions aligned with US policy) gives policymakers leverage to implement comprehensive, targeted sanctions and controls on upstream suppliers to restrict flows to Iran, strengthening sanctions enforcement.

Tighter and more frequent export‑control enforcement (licenses, audits, penalties) raises legal/operational risk for multinational suppliers and banks, causing them to stop or curtail transactions that could re‑route sanctioned goods to Iran and thus increase compliance.

Tightened export controls and enforcement on AI-related chips and dual-use electronics quickly disrupt procurement channels and spares flows used in munitions production and repair, reducing on-hand ammunition, guidance units and sustainment stocks in theater.

Tightened export controls or enforcement actions on AI hardware/software produce immediate counterparty stress and price dislocations in affected financial exposures, prompting central banks/treasuries to scale up direct asset purchases and emergency facilities to stabilize markets.

Stronger cross-border enforcement and sanctions increase settlement, compliance and counterparty risk for dealers and foreign holders, causing wider haircuts and pullbacks that materially reduce bid/ask depth in the Treasury market.

Stronger US export controls and enforcement on AI hardware create immediate lobbying and public pressure in Canada from affected firms and labour groups to demand retaliatory or protective economic policies, raising domestic political escalation pressure.

Heightened enforcement and extraterritorial export controls raise compliance risk and potential market access losses for firms operating across the US–Canada boundary, causing companies to scale back or delay bilateral-capital commitments and projects.

nodes.description: The frequency and intensity of disruptive incidents to maritime traffic (attacks, seizures, detentions, mine threats) per unit time.

nodes.label: Export volume from affected suppliers

nodes.label: Global oil inventory levels
nodes.description: The aggregated stock of commercial and strategic crude and fuel inventories held across markets and storage facilities.

nodes.label: Refinery capacity utilization
nodes.description: The proportion of refining infrastructure throughput in operation relative to installed capacity, affecting refined product supply.

nodes.label: Financial market volatility
nodes.description: The magnitude of short‑term price fluctuations across major financial asset classes (equities, bonds, FX, commodities, crypto).

nodes.label: Capital outflow rate from targeted economy
nodes.description: The rate at which financial capital leaves the economy under pressure (bank withdrawals, asset sales, cross‑border flows) per unit time.

nodes.label: Secondary sanctions risk

nodes.label: Regional diplomatic activity

nodes.label: Domestic unrest intensity
nodes.description: The level of civil disruption within the affected population, including protests, strikes, panic buying and political instability.

nodes.label: Domestic fuel availability

nodes.label: Retaliatory measure intensity

nodes.label: Bilateral trade volume

nodes.label: Supply chain disruption

nodes.label: Commodity price volatility
nodes.description: Amplitude and frequency of price swings in key commodities sensitive to the dispute (e.g., energy, metals, agricultural goods).

nodes.label: Currency exchange volatility
nodes.description: Magnitude and variability of exchange‑rate movements between the two currencies relevant to bilateral trade and investment.

nodes.label: Inflationary pressure
nodes.description: Upward pressure on general price levels arising from higher import costs, supply constraints, and passthrough effects.

nodes.label: Monetary policy stance
nodes.description: Aggregate direction and intensity of central bank policy (accommodation vs tightening) in response to macro shocks.

nodes.label: Investor sentiment
nodes.description: Aggregate market participants' risk appetite and confidence regarding investments exposed to the bilateral economic relationship.

nodes.label: Capital flow volatility
nodes.description: Variability in cross‑border portfolio and direct investment flows in response to policy and market shocks.

nodes.label: Corporate investment commitment
nodes.description: Level of planned or committed capital expenditures and investment projects in sectors reliant on the bilateral market.

nodes.label: Production capacity utilization
nodes.description: Extent to which manufacturing and processing capacity in exposed sectors is being used relative to potential output.

nodes.label: Logistics and transport congestion
nodes.description: Degree of delay and bottlenecking in ports, rail, and trucking networks supporting bilateral trade flows.

nodes.label: Market volatility index
nodes.description: Overall volatility in financial markets (equities, credit, derivatives) reflecting uncertainty tied to the dispute.

nodes.label: Political escalation pressure
nodes.description: Intensity of domestic political forces and public opinion driving increases in confrontational economic policy measures.

nodes.label: Industry lobbying intensity
nodes.description: Strength and frequency of organized private‑sector advocacy aimed at shaping government trade and mitigation policies.

nodes.label: Short-term rate expectations
nodes.description: The market-implied expected path for near-term policy interest rates over the coming months.

nodes.label: Bond market liquidity
nodes.description: The ease and depth with which large bond transactions can be executed without materially moving prices.

nodes.label: Market-making inventory capacity
nodes.description: The aggregate capacity of intermediaries to hold and absorb bond positions for facilitation of trading.

nodes.label: Speculative net positions
nodes.description: The aggregate directional exposure of speculative and leveraged traders in fixed-income instruments relative to hedges.

nodes.label: Options market open interest
nodes.description: The total outstanding number of option contracts on fixed-income underliers that remain unsettled and can drive hedging flows.

nodes.label: Net bond supply flow
nodes.description: The net issuance or retirement of long-term sovereign bonds entering or exiting market circulation per unit time.

nodes.label: Operational cash balance
nodes.description: The level of readily available cash reserves that authorities can deploy for market operations or short-term funding needs.

nodes.label: Market intervention intensity
nodes.description: The rate and scale at which policy actors engage in direct asset purchases or other market-stabilizing operations.

nodes.label: Monetary policy stance
nodes.description: The current orientation of monetary policy considering rates, guidance and balance-sheet posture as perceived by markets.

nodes.label: Inflation rate
nodes.description: The ongoing percentage change in a broad price index measuring the general level of consumer prices.

nodes.label: Inflation momentum
nodes.description: The recent acceleration or deceleration trend in the inflation rate that signals persistence of price pressures.

nodes.label: Cross-border capital flows
nodes.description: The net movement of portfolio and other capital across borders into or out of domestic fixed-income and related markets per unit time.

nodes.label: Exchange rate level
nodes.description: The prevailing value of the domestic currency relative to major foreign currencies, affecting returns and capital allocation.

nodes.label: Market volatility index
nodes.description: A summary measure of expected near-term price variability in fixed-income and related markets.

nodes.label: Political constraint intensity
nodes.description: The degree of political resistance or support that limits or enables discretionary fiscal and market operations.

nodes.label: Infrastructure vulnerability
nodes.description: The susceptibility of critical energy, industrial, transport and retail infrastructure to damage or disruption from attacks or sabotage.

nodes.label: Allied military supply flow
nodes.description: The rate and volume at which external defensive and offensive military materiel, systems and logistical support are delivered into the theater.

nodes.label: Defensive hardening rate
nodes.description: The pace at which physical and technical protective measures (air defences, fortifications, redundancy) are implemented to reduce attack effects.

nodes.label: Intelligence backchannel activity
nodes.description: The intensity of covert and official intelligence, liaison and risk-management communications between adversarial and external security actors.

nodes.label: Dual-use service availability
nodes.description: The operational capacity and accessibility of private-sector dual-use services (communications, satellite, logistics platforms) for wartime use.

nodes.label: Battlefield data sharing intensity
nodes.description: The frequency and depth of real-time operational data and targeting information exchanged among cooperating military actors.

nodes.label: Industrial production capacity
nodes.description: The available manufacturing and repair capacity for munitions, vehicles and maintenance in the conflict-relevant industrial base.

nodes.label: Economic disruption level
nodes.description: The aggregate degree of disruption to commerce, energy markets and retail/online trade caused by attacks, sanctions and logistical breakdowns.

nodes.label: Mobilization readiness
nodes.description: The state of force generation capacity, reserve activation potential and logistical readiness to expand military manpower and deployments.

nodes.label: Escalation perception
nodes.description: Stakeholder perceptions of the likelihood and imminence of conflict escalation into a broader or more destructive phase.

nodes.label: Political/legal constraint level
nodes.description: The strength of domestic and international legal, political and institutional limits on direct involvement or escalation by external actors.

nodes.label: Cyber and space asset integrity
nodes.description: The operational health and resilience of cyber, satellite and communications assets that support military and civilian functions.

nodes.label: Logistics and ammunition stocks
nodes.description: The on-hand levels of munitions, fuel, spare parts and transport capacity that sustain ongoing military operations.

nodes.label: Public support level
nodes.description: The aggregate domestic and allied public and political support for continued military engagement and aid provision.

nodes.label: Escalation control measures
nodes.description: The rate at which active diplomatic, confidence-building and de-escalatory interventions are employed to limit conflict escalation.

nodes.label: Capital investment rate
nodes.description: The flow of new financial capital being allocated to AI infrastructure, data centers, hardware production and related projects.

nodes.label: Sector debt exposure
nodes.description: The stock level of leverage and outstanding debt taken on to finance AI infrastructure and firms within the ecosystem.

nodes.label: Hardware manufacturing capacity
nodes.description: The installed and producible supply capacity for AI accelerators, chips and supporting hardware in the ecosystem.

nodes.label: Market concentration
nodes.description: The degree to which production, supply or procurement of AI infrastructure is concentrated among a small number of suppliers or buyers.

nodes.label: Accelerator hardware price level
nodes.description: The prevailing price level for key AI hardware (accelerators, high-end GPUs, racks) adjusted for performance and supply conditions.

nodes.label: Custom silicon development rate
nodes.description: The pace at which new custom accelerators and custom silicon solutions are designed, validated and brought toward production.

nodes.label: Data-center buildout rate
nodes.description: The speed of physical deployment of data-center capacity, colocation racks and supporting infrastructure per unit time.

nodes.label: Talent mobility rate
nodes.description: The rate at which skilled workers, engineers and researchers move between firms, sectors and geographies within the AI ecosystem.

nodes.label: Executive turnover rate
nodes.description: The frequency of senior-executive departures, hires and role changes among organizations that shape AI infrastructure strategy.

nodes.label: Regulatory enforcement intensity
nodes.description: The strength and frequency of enforcement actions, export controls and compliance interventions targeting AI-related goods and activities.

nodes.label: Illicit trade/smuggling rate
nodes.description: The rate of illegal or circumventing flows of restricted AI hardware and components across borders and through informal channels.

nodes.label: Supply-chain resilience
nodes.description: The ability of the AI hardware and infrastructure supply chain to absorb disruptions and restore normal throughput over time.

nodes.label: Regulatory uncertainty perception
nodes.description: The market and industry perception of unpredictability and ambiguity in rules, export regimes and enforcement related to AI infrastructure.

nodes.label: Investor confidence/sentiment
nodes.description: The prevailing sentiment of investors toward the AI infrastructure sector, reflected in risk appetite, valuations and financing willingness.

nodes.label: Compute consumption centralization
nodes.description: The extent to which AI compute demand is concentrated in a few large consumers versus dispersed across many users and firms.

Broad economic disruption from sanctions, commodity shocks and disrupted trade routes depresses demand and raises costs for exporters and importers, reducing the flow of goods and services between the US and Canada as firms cut orders and postpone shipments.
Rising perceptions of imminent escalation prompt central banks and treasuries to deploy preemptive bond purchases, liquidity facilities and swap lines to calm funding strains and tail-risk concerns.

Rising perception that the conflict may broaden increases domestic political pressure in both countries to take hardline economic positions (use trade tools for leverage, restrict sensitive transfers), intensifying confrontational rhetoric and demands for retaliatory trade measures in bilateral disputes.

Rising perceptions that the Russia–Ukraine conflict may broaden prompt US/EU policymakers to expand and more actively enforce export controls and sanctions on advanced computing and semiconductors destined for China to limit dual‑use spillovers.

Depletion of ammunition, fuel and spare parts in the Ukraine theater drives covert procurement from sanctioned sources, creating commercial opportunities that lead intermediaries, shippers and banks to loosen compliance and facilitate sanction‑circumventing transactions.

Persistent depletion of ammunition and logistics stocks forces defense prime contractors and tiered suppliers to retool capacity and prioritize urgent domestic contracts, prompting them to delay or cancel planned cross‑border capital projects and investments in Canada.

A sharp rise in demand for advanced AI compute raises the perceived dual‑use risk of high‑end chips and accelerators, prompting governments to expand the scope and tightness of sanctions/export controls that can be applied to Iran to prevent military/AI applications.

Sustained inflows of capital into non‑Western chip/hardware production and alternative finance in China and allied markets create viable suppliers and payment channels that third parties can use to evade Western restrictions, reducing overall compliance with sanctions on Iran.
A surge of capital into onshoring AI hardware and supply-chain capacity in the US redirects procurement away from Canadian suppliers, directly reducing bilateral goods and component trade flows.

An increase in global AI accelerator and vision-processor manufacturing capacity lowers unit costs and expands availability of components used in loitering munitions, comms/autonomy kits and seekers, enabling faster fielding or replenishment of UAV/precision strike stocks and thus raising the tempo of kinetic strikes.

A fall in producible AI hardware capacity (e.g., curtailed chip output) directly produces component shortages that force rerouting, delays and higher transaction costs across North American supply chains, increasing US–Canada supply disruptions (conversely, capacity growth reduces disruption).

Greater concentration of critical AI/hardware supply in a few firms (especially in jurisdictions aligned with US policy) gives policymakers leverage to implement comprehensive, targeted sanctions and controls on upstream suppliers to restrict flows to Iran, strengthening sanctions enforcement.

Tighter and more frequent export‑control enforcement (licenses, audits, penalties) raises legal/operational risk for multinational suppliers and banks, causing them to stop or curtail transactions that could re‑route sanctioned goods to Iran and thus increase compliance.

Tightened export controls and enforcement on AI-related chips and dual-use electronics quickly disrupt procurement channels and spares flows used in munitions production and repair, reducing on-hand ammunition, guidance units and sustainment stocks in theater.

Tightened export controls or enforcement actions on AI hardware/software produce immediate counterparty stress and price dislocations in affected financial exposures, prompting central banks/treasuries to scale up direct asset purchases and emergency facilities to stabilize markets.

Stronger cross-border enforcement and sanctions increase settlement, compliance and counterparty risk for dealers and foreign holders, causing wider haircuts and pullbacks that materially reduce bid/ask depth in the Treasury market.

Stronger US export controls and enforcement on AI hardware create immediate lobbying and public pressure in Canada from affected firms and labour groups to demand retaliatory or protective economic policies, raising domestic political escalation pressure.

Heightened enforcement and extraterritorial export controls raise compliance risk and potential market access losses for firms operating across the US–Canada boundary, causing companies to scale back or delay bilateral-capital commitments and projects.
